'''Dianne Kasnic Prinz''' (September 29, 1938 – October 12, 2002) was an American scientist, a physicist with the [[United States Naval Research Laboratory]]. She trained as an astronaut, and was mission communicator for [[STS-51-F]].

== Early life and education ==
Dianne Kasnic was born in [[Economy, Pennsylvania]], the daughter of Joseph J. Kasnic and Anna Mae Kosyrich Kasnic. Her father was a farmer, steelworker and coal miner.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Zielinski |first=Graeme |date=October 19, 2002 |title=Dianne K. Prinz |newspaper=The Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/2002/10/19/dianne-k-prinz/6599f052-f26b-49a5-b62e-d351ddc5ba9e/ |access-date=March 23, 2022}}</ref><ref name=":11">{{Cite news |last=Peterson |first=Karen |date=1978-11-19 |title=Female Physicist Undaunted by Spacelab Assignment |pages=45 |work=The Pantagraph |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/98221037/female-physicist-undaunted-by-spacelab/ |access-date=2022-03-23 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> "My father always appreciated scientific things, even though he only went to the seventh grade," she explained in 1978. "We had a small farm and there were lots of chemicals around so I got interested in chemistry."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Boodman |first=Sandra G. |date=1978-08-24 |title=Spacelab 2 |language=en-US |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1978/08/24/spacelab-2/c15b1e7a-b80a-4117-a96d-ad576f00a9a5/ |access-date=2022-03-23 |issn=0190-8286}}</ref> She graduated from [[Ambridge Area High School]] in 1956,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Prinz, Dianne Kasnic |url=https://www.ambridge.k12.pa.us/?p=9341 |access-date=2022-03-23 |website=Ambridge Area School District| date=June 2019 }}</ref><ref name=":10">{{Cite news |last=Rankin |first=Edwina |date=1979-03-31 |title=Spacelab Scientist Sends Area Pupils into Orbit |pages=2 |work=The Pittsburgh Press |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/98219552/spacelab-scientist-sends-area-pupils/ |access-date=2022-03-23 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> and  the [[University of Pittsburgh]] in 1960. She earned a PhD in physics at [[Johns Hopkins University]] in 1967.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Cook |first1=John William |last2=Howard |first2=Russell Alfred |date=2003-12-01 |title=Obituary: Dianne K. Prinz, 1938-2002 |url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2003BAAS...35.1469C |journal=Bulletin of the American Astronomical Society |volume=35 |issue=5 |pages=1469–1470|bibcode=2003BAAS...35.1469C }}</ref> Her dissertation was titled "Strength-half-width Products of Self-broadened Lines in the 6.3 Micron Band of [[Water vapor|Water Vapor]]".<ref>Dianne (Kasnic) Prinz. ''Strength-half-width Products of Self-broadened Lines in the 6.3 Micron Band of Water Vapor''. Johns Hopkins University, Laboratory of Astrophysics and Physical Meteorology, 1966.</ref>

== Career ==
Prinz was a postdoctoral fellow at the [[University of Maryland, College Park|University of Maryland]] from 1967 to 1971. In 1971, she joined the Naval Research Laboratory as a research physicist. Her title at retirement  in 2000 was Head of the Solar Radiation Section, Solar Physics Branch, Space Science Division of the Naval Research Laboratory. Much of her work involved studies of [[solar irradiance]]. She was a volunteer for the Navy Community Outreach Program, speaking to students and community groups about the laboratory's work.<ref name=":0" /> She was a fellow of the Washington Academy of Science, and vice president of the National Capital Section of the [[Optica (society)|Optical Society of America]].<ref name=":1" /> 

Prinz trained as an astronaut beginning in 1978,<ref name=":10" /> the first woman trained by NASA as a payload specialist. She was often mentioned as a possible "first American woman in space,"<ref name=":11" /><ref name=":10" /><ref>{{Cite news |date=1978-08-13 |title=Woman Could Go Into Space |pages=33 |work=The Times |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/98220712/woman-could-go-into-space/ |access-date=2022-03-23 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> but she never went into space. She was mission communicator for the [[STS-51-F|Spacelab 2]] mission in 1985,<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |date=November–December 1978 |title=Naval Research Lab Woman Chosen for Spacelab Project |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8CJBwENUGAsC&dq=Dianne%20Prinz%20Women%20in%20Action%201978&pg=RA1-PA6 |journal=Women in Action |volume=8 |pages=6}}</ref> supporting the [[Upper Atmosphere Research Satellite|SUSIM-UARS]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wayne |first=Tiffany K. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gPGZJ_YuMwgC&dq=Dianne+Kasnic&pg=PA773 |title=American Women of Science Since 1900 |date=2011 |publisher=ABC-CLIO |isbn=978-1-59884-158-9 |pages=773–774 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Floyd |first1=L. E. |last2=Cook |first2=J. W. |last3=Herring |first3=L. C. |last4=Crane |first4=P. C. |date=2003-05-01 |title=SUSIM'S 11-year observational record of the solar UV irradiance |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0273117703001480 |journal=Advances in Space Research |series=Chemistry, Dynamics and Layered Structures of the Atmosphere |language=en |volume=31 |issue=9 |pages=2111–2120 |doi=10.1016/S0273-1177(03)00148-0 |bibcode=2003AdSpR..31.2111F |issn=0273-1177|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Prinz shared in the Navy Award of Merit for Group Achievement in 1985, and the NASA Public Service Group Achievement Award in 1987. She received the [[Navy Meritorious Civilian Service Award]] in 2001.<ref name=":1" />

== Personal life ==
Dianne Kasnic married fellow scientist Gary Prinz; they later divorced. Dianne K. Prinz died from cancer in 2002, aged 64 years, in [[Arlington County, Virginia|Arlington, Virginia]].<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Croft |first1=Melvin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rL6GDwAAQBAJ&dq=Dianne+Kasnic&pg=PA136 |title=Come Fly with Us: NASA's Payload Specialist Program |last2=Youskauskas |first2=John |date=2019-02-01 |publisher=U of Nebraska Press |isbn=978-1-4962-1226-9 |pages=136 |language=en}}</ref>
